chapter_title: Concerning the Catechumen who found fault with the Elect: why he is angry
chapter_note: This chapter contains no oldest cosmological-correspondential substrate. It is entirely institutional/pastoral material structured within a dialogue frame. The chapter addresses catechumen-elect community relations — a fundamentally institutional concern. While cosmological concepts are referenced (the two essences, body not one's own, flesh of Sin, divinity from the heights), these are CITED as known doctrine to support pastoral arguments, not TAUGHT as systematic cosmological mappings. The tree analogy in ¶4 is an illustrative simile (tree → the elect), not a cosmic correspondence (both sides do not stay within the cosmic system). Teaching purity score of 0.147 confirms the absence of substrate vocabulary.

paragraphs.temporal_note: Pure formulaic opening: 'Once again, it happened one time' plus institutional terminology ('catechumen', 'apostle'). Dialogue frame score 50.0 confirms. Sets up the narrative scenario.

The catechumen's complaint about the righteous/elect being angry. Entirely pastoral — concerns community behavior and interpersonal dynamics among the elect. No cosmological content. The question is not a substantive cosmological question but a pastoral grievance about institutional members.
Pure dialogue attribution formula: 'Then our enlightener speaks to that catechumen.' Dialogue frame score 57.14 confirms.

Extended tree analogy (scented-oil tree). This is illustrative parable used pastorally, not systematic cosmological correspondence. One side of the mapping is a natural tree; the other is the institutional category of the elect. The analogy serves the pastoral argument about tolerating the elect's flaws. 'Just as this tree...' explicitly marks it as simile, not cosmological mapping.

Applies the tree analogy to the elect. Contains cosmological-flavored language ('gods', 'image of the gods', 'divinity planted in them came from the heights', 'will of the greatness') but all of it serves to describe the status of 'the elect' — an institutional category. The mapping is cosmos → institutional community members, crossing out of the cosmic system.

Pastoral explanation of why the elect get angry. References dualistic anthropology ('body that is not their own', 'flesh of Sin that makes the other dwell in a foreign land') but these are cosmological concepts being APPLIED to explain institutional behavior, not being taught systematically. 'Sin' is personified ('flesh of Sin') — a cosmological reference in service of pastoral instruction.

Pastoral exhortation to the catechumen not to criticize the elect. References 'the mystery of the two essences' and 'what is good and what is evil dwell in every person' — but these are CITED as things the catechumen already knows ('you have known', 'you have understood'), not taught. The cosmological dualism is presupposed background, not the teaching content. The teaching content is pastoral: don't criticize the saints.

Institutional pastoral instruction about catechumen-elect reciprocity. Contains institutional vocabulary: 'sin', 'teacher', 'wisdom of God', 'congregation', 'land of light'. 'Cross of Light' is a Manichaean cosmic term but used in institutional context ('beat the Cross of Light' = harming light through worldly living). The elect's acceptance of the sinful catechumen parallels the catechumen's expected acceptance of the elect's anger. Substrate score 3.27 from 'Cross of Light' and 'land of light' but these are institutional usage of cosmic terms.

Closing moral instruction within the institutional speech. 'Love and honour them. Do not speak against them.' Direct pastoral address to the catechumen. Could be classified as exhortation, but since there is no substrate teaching sequence to which it is appended, it functions as part of the same institutional pastoral discourse.

Narrative transition formula: 'Then, when the apostle had uttered these words to that catechumen, he was persuaded in his heart. He says to him, weeping.' Dialogue frame with institutional vocabulary ('apostle', 'catechumen').

The catechumen's penitent response. References 'the old man too dwells in their body' — dualistic anthropology (the 'old man' dwelling in the body as the source of sin). 'Old man' (palaios anthropos) may reflect Pauline influence adopted into Manichaean vocabulary. The cosmological reference again serves the pastoral/institutional context.
